analysis.one_liner: Funds federal agencies and Ukraine aid, pays wildfire victims; its original insulin price caps were stripped.
analysis.headline: The House passed a $35 insulin copay cap 232-193 in March, but the Senate reused the bill number to pass a stopgap government funding and Ukraine aid package 72-25 in September, replacing the insulin text, and the insulin caps never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill began as the Affordable Insulin Now Act, which capped insulin copays at $35 a month for people with private insurance and Medicare. The House passed it in March 2022. Months later, the Senate took the same bill number, replaced its text with a package that funds federal agencies through mid-December, adds billions in Ukraine aid, and pays victims of a New Mexico wildfire. That funding package became law; the insulin caps never did.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal agencies and their workers, who keep operating instead of a shutdown; low-income households, which get $1 billion in home energy assistance; survivors of the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon wildfire, who get a $2.5 billion compensation program; Ukraine, which gets military and economic aid; veterans programs that were about to expire; and drug and medical device companies, whose FDA user fees are reauthorized through 2027. Defense contractors gain from procurement to replace weapons sent to Ukraine. Insulin users do not benefit: the $35 cap the House passed was removed before the final version.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Program beneficiaries, fire victims, Ukraine, defense contractors

how_it_helps.text: The final law is a continuing resolution that funds federal agencies at fiscal 2022 levels through December 16, 2022, preventing a government shutdown that would have begun October 1.

It creates a compensation program for victims of the Hermit's Peak/Calf Canyon fire in New Mexico, funded with $2.5 billion transferred from FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund, covering personal injury, property loss, business loss, and financial loss.

It provides an additional $1 billion for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, which pays heating bills for low-income households, plus roughly $12 billion in Ukraine-related defense appropriations, $4.5 billion in economic assistance for Ukraine's government, and $1.775 billion for refugee and entrant assistance including unaccompanied minors.

It extends a long list of programs that were about to expire: TANF welfare funding, the Maternal, Infant, and Early Childhood Home Visiting Program, child and family services, homeless veteran programs through 2024, and FDA authority to collect drug, device, generic drug, and biosimilar user fees through fiscal 2027.

The original House-passed bill capped insulin cost-sharing at $35 a month under private insurance and Medicare beginning in 2023, replacing a voluntary Medicare model that was set to expire at the end of 2025.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of the appropriations, and the law designates the new spending as emergency spending exempt from pay-as-you-go budget enforcement. Insulin users bear a cost of omission: the $35 copay cap the House passed 232-193 was dropped, so people with diabetes who use insulin continue to face whatever cost-sharing their insurer sets. Health insurers and insulin manufacturers are spared any new obligation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers; insulin users kept paying uncapped copays

drawbacks.text: The insulin caps that gave the bill its name were entirely removed. The final law, as summarized at passage and at enactment, contains no insulin cost-sharing provision, and the Senate never voted on the House-passed insulin language as a standalone measure.
The law designates its Ukraine and related spending as emergency requirements, exempting it from statutory PAYGO, the Senate PAYGO rule, and other budget scorekeeping rules.

As a stopgap, the continuing resolution holds most programs at fiscal 2022 levels and bars agencies from starting or resuming any project not funded in fiscal 2022, delaying decisions on new priorities.

Part of the Ukraine funding takes the form of procurement and replenishment, including over $9.7 billion in defense-wide procurement and $540 million to expand munitions production plants, which flows to defense suppliers.

The FDA user fee division reauthorizes through fiscal 2027 a funding system in which the agency negotiates its fees with the drug and device industries every five years, keeping those industries as the funders of the regulator that reviews their products.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The funding package delivered real, concrete benefits: a shutdown averted, heating aid for low-income households, a compensation program for people whose homes and businesses burned in a federally caused wildfire, and aid to Ukraine with oversight and reporting requirements attached. The sharpest loss is the insulin copay cap, which passed the House with 232 votes and was never given its own Senate vote; it disappeared when the bill number was converted into a funding vehicle. Weighing the whole law, the benefits to ordinary people are broad but diffuse, while the specific promise many House members voted for in March was never kept.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed a $35 insulin cap bill in March; the Senate later reused the bill number as a vehicle, replaced the insulin text with a government funding and Ukraine aid package, passed that 72-25, the House accepted it 230-201 the next day, and the President signed it into law on September 30, 2022 — with the insulin caps nowhere in the final version.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2022 as the Affordable Insulin Now Act, capping insulin cost-sharing at $35 a month under private insurance and Medicare, with 31 Democratic cosponsors joining the sponsor.
The House passed the insulin bill on March 31, 2022 by 232-193, with all 220 voting Democrats in favor and 12 Republicans joining them; a Republican motion to recommit failed 197-225.
The House-passed version also delayed implementation of Medicare Part D rebate regulations and increased funding for the Medicare Improvement Fund.
The bill then sat in the Senate for nearly five months, placed on the calendar in May without action.

In late September 2022, with government funding set to lapse, the Senate took up the bill: cloture on a motion to proceed was invoked 72-23 on September 27, and on September 29 the Senate passed the measure 72-25 with an amendment that replaced the insulin text with a continuing resolution through December 16, Ukraine supplemental appropriations, a New Mexico wildfire compensation program, veterans and health program extensions, and the FDA user fee reauthorization.

The House agreed to the Senate amendment on September 30, 2022 by 230-201, with all 220 voting Democrats in favor and 201 of 212 Republicans opposed, and the President signed it the same day as Public Law 117-180.
The final law contains no insulin cost-sharing provision; the $35 cap lives only in the House-passed version of the bill, which never received a Senate vote of its own.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies, Ukraine, and New Mexico fire victims got their funding, and defense contractors gained procurement work. Insulin manufacturers and health insurers came out ahead too: they face no copay cap, and drug and device companies got their FDA user fees reauthorized through 2027. The people left worse off than the House vote promised are insulin users, who lost the $35 cap without it ever being voted down on its merits.

sides.party_line_note: Final votes split by party: the House passed the package 230-201 with all 220 voting Democrats for and 201 of 212 Republicans against, while the Senate passed it 72-25 with every Democrat and both independents for and Republicans split 22 for, 25 against; the earlier House vote on the insulin bill was 232-193 with 12 Republicans joining.

industries.note: The Ukraine supplemental funds replenishment of U.S. weapons stocks, including over $9.7 billion in defense-wide procurement, $540 million to expand munitions production plants, and $3 billion for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, all of which is spent buying from U.S. defense suppliers. The same money supports Ukraine's defense, a goal most of the public backs, while guaranteeing those companies a new stream of purchases.

The House-passed bill would have capped what insulin users pay at $35 a month; the final law contains no such cap, so manufacturers keep their pricing power over a drug millions depend on. The same law also reauthorizes the FDA user fees the industry pays for its regulators through 2027 under terms negotiated with the industry every five years.

The dropped insulin provision would have limited the cost-sharing insurers can charge insulin users to $35 a month; its removal leaves insurers free to set insulin copays as they choose. Insurers also benefit from the extension of Medicare hospital and rural payment adjustments in the final law.

industries.industry: Drug and medical device makers (FDA user fee system)
industries.note: The law reauthorizes through 2027 the system in which drug, device, generic, and biosimilar companies pay the FDA's review costs, with fee totals negotiated between the agency and the industry every five years. This locks in industry-funded regulation as the permanent way the FDA is financed, while keeping the review process that brings companies' products to market running.
